questions.stem: A competent client says that cultural and religious beliefs make family participation important in end-of-life decisions. What is the nurse's best approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ask the client how family members should be involved, clarify the client's preferences, and incorporate those preferences into care when clinically and legally feasible.","B":"Assume the family should make decisions because clients from cultures that value collective decision-making generally prefer to transfer personal authority to relatives.","C":"Exclude the family from discussions because patient autonomy requires individual decision-making and does not permit culturally preferred family participation.","D":"Ask the oldest family member to decide how information should be shared because age-based hierarchy is the safest way to avoid stereotyping the client's preferences."}}
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive care centers the competent client's stated values and preferences rather than stereotypes. The nurse should ask how the client wants family involved and incorporate those preferences when clinically and legally feasible; the patient retains the right to participate in care planning and informed decisions.
questions.source_name: HHS National CLAS Standards + eCFR Patient Rights
questions.source_detail: HHS National CLAS Standards, Principal Standard 1: respectful care responsive to cultural health beliefs/practices and communication needs; Think Cultural Health current standards page reviewed 2026-08-15. Cross-check: 42 CFR §482.13(b)(1)-(2) gives the patient the right to participate in the plan of care and make informed decisions; current eCFR reviewed 2026-08-15 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-482/subpart-B/section-482.13).

questions.stem: A client has progressive dyspnea, peripheral edema, and jugular venous distention. The provider orders BNP. How should the nurse understand this test?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An elevated BNP confirms heart failure by itself and removes the need to consider renal function, age, rhythm disorders, imaging findings, or the rest of the clinical picture.","B":"BNP is a useful biomarker that can support the diagnosis and assessment of heart failure, but the value should be interpreted with symptoms, examination, and other testing.","C":"BNP is primarily a marker of pancreatic inflammation, so elevation in a client with dyspnea points away from a cardiovascular cause of the current symptoms.","D":"BNP is mainly useful for prognosis after heart failure is established, so it should not be used to support the diagnostic evaluation of a new dyspnea presentation."}}
questions.rationale: The 2026 Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure states that elevated BNP or NT-proBNP can increase diagnostic certainty, but heart failure is established by an accumulation of symptoms, signs, and laboratory or imaging evidence rather than by a single test. BNP therefore supports, but does not independently establish, the diagnosis.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF — Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure (2026)
questions.source_detail: 2026 AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF Expert Consensus Document, definition of HF syndrome: diagnostic certainty is amplified by elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, while HF is defined by an accumulation of suggestive features in comprehensive assessment rather than a single diagnostic test. Published online 2026-06-29, DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2026.05.036; reviewed 2026-08-15.
